record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: For federated learning research across cross-device and cross-silo settings, how can the community define standard evaluation metrics and benchmark datasets that are representative of real-world federated deployments, including non-IID, unbalanced, privacy-sensitive, and scale-sensitive conditions?

evidence.quote: Developing standard evaluation metrics and establishing standard benchmark datasets

artifact.self_contained_problem: Federated learning is a distributed machine-learning paradigm in which a collection of clients (e.g., mobile devices in cross-device settings, or institutions in cross-silo settings) collaboratively train a shared model under the coordination of a server, while each client's raw data remains local. Realistic federated deployments exhibit several characteristic conditions: (i) non-IID data, meaning that local data distributions P_i differ across clients i; (ii) unbalanced data, meaning that the number of samples n_i per client varies substantially; (iii) privacy-sensitivity, meaning that messages exchanged between clients and server should leak as little information about local data as possible (e.g., under formal notions such as differential privacy); and (iv) scale-sensitivity, meaning that the number of participating clients N may range from tens to millions and only a small subset participates per round.\n\nProblem. Propose and justify (a) a suite of standard quantitative evaluation metrics M = {m_1, …, m_k} jointly measuring predictive accuracy/utility, communication cost, computation cost, fairness across clients, privacy leakage, robustness to client dropout, and robustness to adversarial or Byzantine participants; and (b) a collection of benchmark datasets D = {D_1, …, D_r} together with explicit client-partitioning procedures so that the resulting federated tasks faithfully represent the non-IID, unbalanced, privacy-sensitive, and scale-sensitive conditions encountered in real cross-device and cross-silo deployments. Establish formal definitions of each m_j (including the precise probabilistic or information-theoretic quantity being measured) and prove that the partitioning procedures generating D_1, …, D_r produce client distributions whose heterogeneity, imbalance, and scale span ranges representative of practical federated systems.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a community-wide open challenge rather than a formal theorem. While various benchmarks (LEAF, FedScale, FLAIR, FedML, pFL-Bench) and metric proposals have appeared since 2019, there is no universally adopted standard set of metrics and datasets covering all the listed real-world conditions; the problem remains open as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: FedScale: Benchmarking Model and System Performance of Federated Learning at Scale
status_evidence.snippet: FedScale provides realistic datasets and an evaluation platform for federated learning across diverse tasks and scales.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress: benchmark suites have been proposed but no single standard is universally adopted.

status_evidence.title: LEAF: A Benchmark for Federated Settings
status_evidence.snippet: LEAF is a modular benchmarking framework for learning in federated settings with open-source datasets and reference implementations.
status_evidence.claim: Early benchmark efforts exist but do not span all real-world conditions.

status_evidence.title: pFL-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Personalized Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: A comprehensive benchmark covering twelve datasets with heterogeneous partitions.
status_evidence.claim: Ongoing benchmark development indicates the problem is not yet definitively settled.
